chapters.title: Life
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, life is not just being alive: it is the full, flowing, God-given life that he wants to share with us
chapters.trueMeaning: Full, flowing life that comes from God
chapters.nutshell: We usually think of life as the time between birth and death, and of eternal life as endless time in heaven. The Hebrew word *chayyim* is plural in form and speaks of life in all its fullness: health, family, blessing and closeness to the living God. The New Testament's *zōē* carries the same idea, and “eternal life” is first of all the life of God's coming age, which can begin now.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical life is the overflowing life of the living God, given as a gift, chosen daily, and finally completed in the resurrection.

Nefesh can mean a person's life, and life is in the blood

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: In English, **life** usually means being alive in the body, or the years between birth and death. We speak of “a long life” or “my life story”. When Christians hear **eternal life**, many picture a soul living for endless time in heaven after death.

The Bible's words are richer. In Hebrew, life is not just a heartbeat or a number of years. It is **fullness**: health, strength, family, food, peace and, above all, nearness to God, who is called “the fountain of life”. In the Greek New Testament, the word chosen for this life is *zōē*, and “eternal life” describes the life of God's new age, which can begin today.

sections.h: Chayyim: life in the plural
p: The usual Hebrew word for life is *chayyim* (חַיִּים). It is always **plural in form**, like *mayim* (water) and *shamayim* (heavens). Grammarians explain this as a plural for something large or many-sided. Jewish teachers sometimes draw a lesson from it: life is never only one thing. That lesson is a preacher's point, not a rule of grammar, but it fits how the Bible speaks.

Moses sets two roads before Israel: “I have set before you **life** and death, blessing and curse. Therefore **choose life**, that you and your offspring may live, loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life” (Deuteronomy 30:19–20). Here life means a whole way of living with God, not only staying alive.

The same word appears in the first pages of the Bible. God breathed into the man “the breath of **life**” (*nishmat chayyim*), and he became a living being (Genesis 2:7). In the garden stood “the tree of **life**” (Genesis 2:9). Later, wisdom is called “a tree of life to those who lay hold of her” (Proverbs 3:18). The psalmist says to God, “With you is the **fountain of life**; in your light do we see light” (Psalm 36:9).

sections.h: Chai and chayah: the living God and living water
p: The adjective *chai* (חַי) means **alive, living**. God is “the living God” (Deuteronomy 5:26; Jeremiah 10:10), and the psalmist thirsts “for God, for the **living** God” (Psalm 42:2). People swore oaths with the words “As the LORD **lives**” (*chai YHWH*, Ruth 3:13; 1 Samuel 14:39). Unlike idols, Israel's God acts, speaks and gives life.

*Chai* is also used for water. In Hebrew, fresh spring water or running water is called *mayim chayyim*, **“living water”**. Isaac's servants found “a well of springing water” (Genesis 26:19, KJV), literally “a well of living water”. God complains that his people “have forsaken me, the fountain of **living waters**” (Jeremiah 2:13). Moving water is living; still, stale water is not.

The verb *chayah* (חָיָה) means **to live**, and in other forms **to keep alive, to revive, to give life**. God asks Ezekiel, “Son of man, can these bones **live**?” (Ezekiel 37:3). Obeying God's ways is the path of life: “if a person does them, he shall **live** by them” (Leviticus 18:5), and “the righteous shall **live** by his faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). The Jewish daily prayer, the Amidah, praises God as the one who **gives life to the dead** (*mechayeh metim*).

sections.h: Nefesh: life in the blood, and life for ever
p: Another Hebrew word often means “life”: *nefesh* (נֶפֶשׁ), the living person or living being. “The **life** of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11), so blood belongs to God (Genesis 9:4). The law of justice says “**life** for life” (*nefesh tachat nafesh*, Exodus 21:23). *Nefesh* is the same word often translated “soul”, which shows that in Hebrew the “soul” is the living self, not a separate ghost.

Near the end of the Hebrew Bible comes a clear promise of resurrection: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to **everlasting life** (*chayei olam*), and some to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). *Olam* means a long, hidden age, often “for ever”. This phrase became the root of the later Jewish hope for *olam ha-ba*, **“the world to come”**.
> In the Hebrew Bible, the opposite of life is not only the moment of death. Sickness, loneliness, oppression and distance from God are all a shrinking of life. Salvation is God giving life back.

sections.h: The Greek words: zōē, bios and psychē
p: When Jewish scholars translated the Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they usually rendered *chayyim* with *zōē* (ζωή) and *nefesh* with *psychē* (ψυχή). Greek also has a third word, *bios* (βίος). English uses “life” for all three, but they are different.

*Zōē* is **life itself**, the state of being alive. John uses it for God's own life: “In him was **life**, and the life was the light of men” (John 1:4). Jesus says, “I am the resurrection and the **life**” (John 11:25), and “I came that they may have **life** and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). The verb is *zaō* (ζάω), “to live”: “Man shall not **live** by bread alone” (Matthew 4:4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3). A related verb, *zōopoieō* (ζωοποιέω), means **to make alive**: “in Christ shall all be **made alive**” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

*Bios* is **life as it is lived**: a lifespan, a way of life, or the means to live. The poor widow put in “all she had to live on” (*holon ton bion autēs*, Mark 12:44). The prodigal son's father divided “his property” (*ton bion*, Luke 15:12). John warns against “the pride of **life**” (*tou biou*, 1 John 2:16), the showy pride in possessions. *Psychē* is one's own life or self: “the good shepherd lays down his **life** for the sheep” (John 10:11).

sections.h: Zōē aiōnios: the life of the age to come
p: The famous phrase **eternal life** is *zōē aiōnios* (ζωὴ αἰώνιος). The adjective comes from *aiōn* (αἰών), “age”. Jews in Jesus' day spoke of two ages: **this age** and **the age to come** (Jesus uses this language in Matthew 12:32). The Mishnah says, “All Israel have a share in **the world to come**” (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). So “eternal life” is first the **life of the coming age**, God's new creation life. It is also never-ending, but that is not all it means.

The rich man asks, “What good deed must I do to have **eternal life**?” Jesus answers, “If you would **enter life**, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:16–17). Here “eternal life” and “life” are the same thing: life in God's coming kingdom.

John adds something wonderful: this life can **begin now**. “And this is eternal life, that they **know** you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). “Whoever has the Son has **life**” (1 John 5:12). Eternal life is a relationship with the living God that starts today and will be completed at the resurrection.

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: **One English word for many.** English has only “life”, so *zōē* (life itself) and *bios* (livelihood) look the same. In 1 John, “the pride of life” (2:16, *bios*) and “whoever has the Son has life” (5:12, *zōē*) use different words. Translators keep “life” because it reads naturally, but the difference between God's life and a person's possessions can be lost. Newer versions help with phrases like “all she had to live on” (NIV, Mark 12:44) where the KJV has “all her living”.

**Life or soul?** *Nefesh* and *psychē* can mean “life” or “soul”. In Leviticus 17:11 the KJV says “the **life** of the flesh is in the blood… to make an atonement for your **souls**”, though both words are *nefesh*. In the KJV Jesus says “whosoever will save his **life** shall lose it” and then “what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own **soul**?” (Matthew 16:25–26), though both are *psychē*. Translators choose by context, which is reasonable, but readers then miss that the “soul” is simply the living person.

**Running water, living water.** The KJV rightly translates *mayim chayyim* as “running water” in Leviticus 14:5, because that is what it means. But English readers then miss the link when Jesus offers the Samaritan woman “**living water**” (John 4:10). She first thought he meant fresh spring water; he meant the life of God's Spirit (John 7:38–39).

**“Eternal” and “everlasting”.** The KJV says “**everlasting life**” in John 3:16; most modern versions say “eternal life”. Both come through the Latin Bible's *vita aeterna*, which shaped English Christian vocabulary. They are true, since this life never ends, but they point mainly to **length of time**. The Greek and Hebrew background points also to the **kind** of life: the life of God's age.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In Jewish life, the word *chayyim* is everywhere. The common toast is *L'chaim!*, **“To life!”** The word *chai* is written with two letters whose number value is 18, so many Jews give gifts in multiples of 18 as a wish for life. When the Torah scroll is returned to the ark in the synagogue, the people sing Proverbs 3:18: “She is a **tree of life** to those who hold fast to her.” At the New Year and on Yom Kippur, prayers ask God to “write us in the **book of life**” (compare Psalm 69:28).

Life is so precious that saving it overrides almost every other rule. The Mishnah teaches that where there is doubt about a life, it **overrides the Sabbath** (Mishnah Yoma 8:6), and that whoever saves one life is counted as if he saved **a whole world** (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). Jesus asks the same question: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” (Mark 3:4).

In the Greco-Roman world, *bios* was the word for a person's life story. Ancient biographies, such as Plutarch's *Lives*, were called *bioi*. That is where our word “biography” comes from. Greek thinkers argued about the best *bios*, the best way to live. Many Greeks pictured the dead as weak shadows in the underworld. Against this, the apostles proclaimed *zōē*: the living God's own life, given to people and leading to bodily resurrection.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: life that starts now
p: Jesus speaks of life as something he **gives**, not something we earn by escaping the body. He heals the sick, raises the dead and welcomes outsiders, and in each act life flows back. “I am the bread of **life**” (John 6:35). “I came that they may have **life**” (John 10:10).

Paul calls the Holy Spirit “the Spirit of **life**” (Romans 8:2) and says that the Spirit “will also give life to your mortal bodies” (Romans 8:11). Baptism means we “walk in **newness of life**” (Romans 6:4). This is not a future in the clouds only. It is the life of the age to come breaking into this age now, and it ends not in a bodiless heaven but in **resurrection** and a renewed creation.

sections.h: Living it out
p: **Choose life every day.** In Deuteronomy, choosing life means loving God, listening to his voice and holding fast to him. Ask each morning: which choices today lead toward life, for me and for others?

**Protect and honour life.** If saving one life is like saving a world, then every person you meet matters. Feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, standing up for the weak and caring for children are ways of sharing God's life. Like the poor widow, you can give your *bios*, what you live on, because you trust the God who gives *zōē*.
**Know God now.** Eternal life begins with knowing the Father and the Son. Prayer, Scripture and fellowship are not duties to fill time; they are drinking from “the fountain of living waters”.

It is only used of animals

chapters.title: Will and Desire
chapters.subtitle: God's “will” in the Bible is less a hidden blueprint and more what delights him, freely shared with willing people
chapters.nutshell: In English, “will” can sound like a cold decree, a hidden plan for your life, or a power of choice that philosophers argue about. The Hebrew *ratson* means what pleases, what is accepted, what someone delights in, and *chafetz* means to take pleasure in something. When Jesus prays “Your will be done”, he is asking that what delights the Father would happen on earth as it does in heaven.
chapters.bigIdea: God's will is his loving delight and purpose, and he invites people to share it freely and gladly, not under force.
skeleton: We picture God's will as a hidden map or a fixed decree
Ratson: favour, acceptance, what pleases
Chafetz: delight; God delights in mercy and life, not death
Avah, nadav and bachar: being willing, volunteering and choosing
Greek thelēma, boulē and eudokia: wish, purpose and good pleasure
Translators choose “will”, “acceptable” or “favour”, each with gains and losses
Jewish prayer says “May it be your will” and asks God to accept our words
Doing God's will means sharing his delight with a willing heart

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: The English word **will** has several meanings. It can be the power to choose (“free will”), a firm decision (“against my will”), or a legal document written before death. When Christians speak of **God's will**, many imagine a hidden plan for their life, like a secret map they must find, or a fixed decree that cannot be changed.

The Bible's words are warmer. In Hebrew, God's will is above all **what pleases him, what he delights in**. It is personal, like a father's wish for his children or a king's favour toward a loyal servant. Much of it is not hidden at all: God has told us what he loves, such as justice, mercy, faithfulness and life.

sections.h: Ratson: favour, acceptance and pleasure
p: The main Hebrew word is *ratson* (רָצוֹן), from the verb *ratsah* (רָצָה), “to be pleased with, to accept”. Its basic picture is **acceptance and favour**. An offering brought rightly is “accepted” before the LORD: the worshipper brings it “that he may be **accepted** before the LORD” (*lirtsono*, Leviticus 1:3). In the royal court, “a servant who deals wisely has the king's **favour**” (Proverbs 14:35), and “his **favour** is like the clouds that bring the spring rain” (Proverbs 16:15).

So when *ratson* is translated “will”, it means **what pleases God**. The psalmist prays, “I delight to do your **will**, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8), and “Teach me to do your **will**, for you are my God!” (Psalm 143:10). The same word can mean the desire of a creature: God opens his hand and “satisfies the **desire** of every living thing” (Psalm 145:16).

Isaiah announces “the year of the LORD's **favour**” (*shenat ratson*, Isaiah 61:2), a time of release like the Jubilee. Jesus read this very passage in the synagogue at Nazareth and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:19–21).

sections.h: Chafetz: what God delights in
p: The verb *chafetz* (חָפֵץ) means **to delight in, to take pleasure in, to desire**. The noun *chefetz* means delight or desire. The blessed person is the one whose “**delight** is in the law of the LORD” (Psalm 1:2). In Psalm 40:8 both words stand side by side: “To do your *ratson*, my God, I *delight*.”

This word shows us God's heart. “Have I any **pleasure** in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). “I have no **pleasure** in the death of anyone… so turn, and live” (Ezekiel 18:32). And through Hosea: “I **desire** steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6), words Jesus quoted twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).
> When the Bible tells us what God “wills”, it is often telling us what he enjoys: mercy, faithfulness, repentance and life.

sections.h: Avah, nadav, bachar and etsah: willing, freewill, choice and counsel
p: *Avah* (אָבָה) means **to be willing, to consent**. Strikingly, it is used mostly with “not”: people “would not”. God says, “If you are **willing** and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land” (Isaiah 1:19), but also, “In returning and rest you shall be saved… But you were **unwilling**” (Isaiah 30:15). Once it is used of God's mercy: “the LORD was **unwilling** to destroy you” (Deuteronomy 10:10). Jesus' lament carries the same sadness: “How often would I have gathered your children… and you were **not willing**!” (Matthew 23:37).

*Nadav* (נָדַב) means **to offer freely, to volunteer**. When the Tabernacle was built, “everyone whose spirit **moved him**” brought gifts, and the people brought “a **freewill offering** to the LORD” (*nedavah*, Exodus 35:21, 29). Deborah sings that “the people offered themselves **willingly**” (Judges 5:2). David prays, “uphold me with a **willing** spirit” (Psalm 51:12). Psalm 110:3 pictures God's people volunteering gladly “on the day of your power”.

Two more words complete the picture. *Bachar* (בָּחַר) means **to choose**: “choose this day whom you will serve” (Joshua 24:15). *Etsah* (עֵצָה) means **counsel, plan, purpose**: “The **counsel** of the LORD stands forever” (Psalm 33:11), and “Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the **purpose** of the LORD that will stand” (Proverbs 19:21).

sections.h: The Greek words: thelēma, boulē and eudokia
p: The most common Greek word is *thelō* (θέλω), “to want, to wish, to will”, and its noun *thelēma* (θέλημα), “what is wanted, will”. The Septuagint uses *thelēma* both for *ratson* (Psalm 40:8, numbered 39:9 in the Greek Psalms) and for *chefetz* (Psalm 1:2). So the Greek word carries the Hebrew sense of **delight**. Jesus teaches us to pray, “Your **will** be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10), and in Gethsemane he prays, “not as I **will**, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).

*Boulomai* (βούλομαι) and *boulē* (βουλή) mean **to intend** and **plan, purpose, counsel**. The Septuagint often uses *boulē* for *etsah*. Peter says Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite **plan** and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and Paul speaks of God “who works all things according to the **counsel** of his will” (Ephesians 1:11). Yet Luke says the Pharisees “rejected the **purpose** of God for themselves” (Luke 7:30). In classical Greek *boulomai* was often the more deliberate word, but in the New Testament the two verbs overlap a great deal.

*Eudokia* (εὐδοκία) means **good pleasure, goodwill, delight**. At the baptism of Jesus the Father says, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am **well pleased**” (*eudokēsa*, Matthew 3:17). Many scholars hear an echo of Isaiah 42:1, “my chosen, in whom my soul **delights**”, where the Hebrew verb is *ratsah*. Paul says God “works in you, both **to will** and to work for his **good pleasure**” (Philippians 2:13). There is also *hekousiōs* (ἑκουσίως), **willingly**, the Septuagint's word for a freewill offering (Psalm 54:6), which Peter uses for elders who serve “**willingly**, as God would have you” (1 Peter 5:2).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: **“Will” or “delight”?** English has no single word that means both “will” and “pleasure”. Translators use “will” for *ratson* and *thelēma* because it fits sentences like “Your will be done”. The Latin Bible's *voluntas* (“fiat voluntas tua”, Matthew 6:10) made “will” the standard church word. But English “will” sounds like a decision or a decree, and the warm Hebrew sense of **what pleases God** can fade.

**“Acceptable” or “favour”?** For Isaiah 61:2 the KJV has “the **acceptable** year of the LORD”, while the NIV and ESV say “the year of the LORD's **favor**”. The Greek translators chose *dektos*, “acceptable”, and Luke 4:19 kept it. Both are faithful to *ratson*, which means acceptance and favour. Older readers could hear “acceptable” as “pleasing to God”; today it sounds like “good enough”, so modern versions say “favour”.

**Freewill people.** In Psalm 110:3 the KJV says “Thy people shall be **willing** in the day of thy power”, while the ESV says “Your people will **offer themselves freely**”. The Hebrew *nedavot* is the plural of the word for freewill offerings. The ESV makes the picture of volunteers and gifts clearer; the KJV keeps the idea of a willing heart.

**Goodwill to whom?** In Luke 2:14 the KJV reads “on earth peace, **good will toward men**”, while the NIV reads “peace to those **on whom his favor rests**”. The difference is not theology but manuscripts: older Greek copies have *eudokias* (“of good pleasure”), later ones *eudokia*, one letter less. Either way the angels announce God's delight and favour toward people. In Ephesians 1:5 the KJV keeps “the **good pleasure** of his will”, while the ESV has “the **purpose** of his will”; the shorter wording reads easily but loses some of the warmth of *eudokia*.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In the ancient Near East, everything at court depended on **the king's favour**. A servant waited to see whether the king would accept him or his gift. Israel's worship used the same language: a sacrifice without blemish was brought so that it would be **accepted** (*ratson*) before God (Leviticus 22:20–21). The great freewill offerings for the Tabernacle (Exodus 35) show another side: God's house was built by **volunteers** whose hearts were moved, not by forced labour.

Jewish prayer is full of this vocabulary. Many prayers begin *Yehi ratson*, **“May it be your will…”**, asking that what pleases God would happen. The Amidah has a blessing called *Retzeh*, asking God to **accept** his people and their prayer, and many people end it with Psalm 19:14: “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be **acceptable** (*leratson*) in your sight, O LORD.” The Mishnah teaches, “Do **his will** as if it were your will, so that he may do your will as if it were his will” (Mishnah Avot 2:4), and another saying in Avot urges strength “to do **the will of your Father in heaven**” (compare Matthew 7:21).

In the Greek cities, the *boulē* was the **city council**, and its decrees began with the formula “It seemed good to the council and the people.” The apostles in Jerusalem used similar language: “it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). Many Greek thinkers, especially the Stoics, spoke of an impersonal **fate** that rules everything. The Bible's picture is different: God's will is the **purpose of a person**, a Father who delights, is grieved, and invites response.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: doing the Father's will
p: For Jesus, doing God's will was like food: “My food is to do the **will** of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). Those who do the Father's will are his family: “whoever does the **will** of God, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:35). In Gethsemane, his own will and the Father's will meet in anguish, and he chooses freely: “not as I will, but as you will.”

The apostles tell us plainly much of what God wills. God “desires (*thelei*) all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). He is “not wishing (*boulomenos*) that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9), an echo of Ezekiel 18. “This is the **will** of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). “Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the **will** of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18). Paul asks us to be renewed in mind so that we may discern “what is the will of God, what is **good and acceptable and perfect**” (Romans 12:2).

sections.h: Living it out
p: **Start with what is revealed.** Instead of worrying about a hidden map, begin with what God has said pleases him: “to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). Most of God's will for today is already known.

**Be a volunteer, not a conscript.** God built his house with freewill gifts. Offer your time, money and gifts gladly, “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

**Pray like a child.** Learn to pray, “May it be your will…”, and “Your will be done”. Let your own desires be shaped by what delights the Father, until, as the Psalmist says, you delight to do his will.

chapters.title: Abide and Dwell
chapters.subtitle: From tents and guest rooms to the Tabernacle and the heart: the Bible's words for staying with God
chapters.trueMeaning: Stay, remain, make your home with
chapters.nutshell: “Abide” sounds old-fashioned and passive to many readers. The Hebrew words picture sitting down at home (*yashav*), pitching a tent among people (*shakhan*), staying as a guest under a host's protection (*gur*) and lodging for the night (*lin*). The Greek *menō* means to stay or remain, and John uses it for the friendship between Jesus and his disciples, while *skēnoō* says the Word “pitched his tent” among us.
chapters.bigIdea: The God who pitched his tent among Israel came to live among us in Jesus, and he invites us to stay with him, as guests and as family, for good.
skeleton: “Abide” sounds archaic and passive in modern English
Yashav: to sit, settle and live somewhere
Shakhan and mishkan: God pitches his tent among his people
Gur and lin: staying as a guest and lodging for the night
Sukkah: Israel's yearly reminder of living in booths with God

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: The word **abide** comes from older English Bibles. Today we rarely use it, except in phrases like “I can't abide it” (I can't stand it) or “law-abiding”. When Christians read “Abide in me” (John 15:4), some imagine a quiet, passive feeling, or a special spiritual state that only a few reach.

The Hebrew and Greek words behind “abide” and “dwell” are everyday words about **where you live and with whom you stay**: sitting down at home, pitching a tent, staying overnight with a host, settling in a town or remaining with a friend. The Bible uses these ordinary pictures to describe how God lives with people and how people live with God.

sections.h: Yashav: to sit down and live somewhere
p: The most common verb is *yashav* (יָשַׁב). Its basic meaning is **to sit**, and from that **to stay, to settle, to live** in a place. A king “sits” on his throne, a judge “sits” to judge (Exodus 18:13), and a family “sits” in its land, that is, lives there.

The psalmists long to live in God's presence: “One thing have I asked of the LORD… that I may **dwell** in the house of the LORD all the days of my life” (Psalm 27:4). Psalm 91 opens with two pictures: “He who **dwells** (*yoshev*, sits) in the shelter of the Most High will **abide** in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1).

From this root comes the later Hebrew word *yeshivah* (יְשִׁיבָה), literally “a sitting”, the name for a school of Torah study, where students sit together and learn. Moses says, “Lord, you have been our **dwelling place** (*ma'on*) in all generations” (Psalm 90:1): God himself is Israel's home.

sections.h: Shakhan and mishkan: God pitches his tent
p: *Shakhan* (שָׁכַן) means **to settle, to dwell**, often in a tent. God says, “Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may **dwell** in their midst” (Exodus 25:8). The tent where he dwells is the *mishkan* (מִשְׁכָּן), the **Tabernacle**, literally “dwelling place”. God promises, “I will **dwell** among the people of Israel and will be their God” (Exodus 29:45).

The same root gives *shakhen* (שָׁכֵן), **neighbour**, the person who lives next to you: “Better is a **neighbour** who is near than a brother who is far away” (Proverbs 27:10). So God's dwelling is not distant; he comes to live next door, in the middle of the camp.

Later Jewish teachers used the word *Shekhinah* (שְׁכִינָה), “the dwelling (presence)”, for God's presence among his people. The word is not in the Bible, but it comes from this root. The Mishnah says that when two people sit together and words of Torah pass between them, **the Shekhinah rests between them** (Mishnah Avot 3:2). Compare Jesus: “where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20).

sections.h: Gur and lin: guests and overnight lodging
p: *Gur* (גּוּר) means **to sojourn**, to live somewhere as an outsider or a guest, under someone else's protection. A *ger* (גֵּר) is a sojourner, a resident foreigner. Abraham went down to Egypt “to **sojourn** there” (Genesis 12:10). God commands Israel to love the *ger*, “for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34). David asks, “O LORD, who shall **sojourn** in your tent? Who shall **dwell** on your holy hill?” (Psalm 15:1). He uses *gur* and *shakhan* together: to live with God is to be **his guest**.

In the ancient world a guest in a tent was protected by the host. So the psalmist prays, “Let me **dwell** in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings!” (Psalm 61:4), and confesses, “I am a **sojourner** with you, a guest, like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).

*Lin* (לִין) means **to lodge, to spend the night**. Ruth says to Naomi, “Where you go I will go, and where you **lodge** I will lodge” (Ruth 1:16). In Psalm 91:1 the one who “abides in the shadow of the Almighty” uses a form of *lin*: he spends the night safe in God's shade. And in Psalm 30:5 sorrow is pictured as an overnight visitor: “Weeping may **tarry** for the night, but joy comes with the morning.”

sections.h: Sukkah: living in booths
p: A *sukkah* (סֻכָּה) is a **booth** or temporary hut made of branches. Every autumn, at the Feast of Booths (Sukkot), God commanded Israel: “You shall **dwell** in booths for seven days… that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:42–43). The verb is *yashav* again.

To this day many Jewish families build a sukkah, eat their meals in it and sometimes sleep in it. It reminds them that life is fragile and that God sheltered his people in the wilderness. The prophets used the same picture for hope: God will raise up “the **booth** of David that is fallen” (Amos 9:11), a verse James quotes at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16).
> The God of Israel is not only a God of temples. He is the God of tents and booths, who travels with his people and lives in the middle of their camp.

sections.h: The Greek words: menō, skēnoō, katoikeō, paroikeō and monē
p: *Menō* (μένω) means **to stay, to remain, to continue**. It is used for staying at someone's home. When two disciples meet Jesus, they ask, “Rabbi, where are you **staying**?” He says, “Come and you will see,” and “they **stayed** with him that day” (John 1:38–39). Jesus tells Zacchaeus, “today I must **stay** at your house” (Luke 19:5), and the Emmaus travellers urge him, “**Stay** with us, for it is toward evening” (Luke 24:29). So when Jesus says, “**Abide** in me, and I in you” (John 15:4), he uses the language of **hospitality and friendship**.

*Skēnoō* (σκηνόω) means **to pitch a tent, to live in a tent**, from *skēnē* (σκηνή), tent. The Septuagint used *skēnē* for the Tabernacle and for the booths of Sukkot. John writes, “the Word became flesh and **dwelt** (*eskēnōsen*, pitched his tent) among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). Readers who knew the Scriptures would think of the Tabernacle filled with God's glory (Exodus 40:34). Some scholars also note that *skēnē* sounds like the Hebrew *shakhan*; whether or not John meant that, his meaning clearly echoes the *mishkan*. At the end, “the **dwelling place** (*skēnē*) of God is with man. He will **dwell** with them” (Revelation 21:3).

*Katoikeō* (κατοικέω) means **to settle down, to live permanently** in a place: Paul prays “that Christ may **dwell** in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:17). Its opposite is *paroikeō* (παροικέω), **to live as a sojourner**; Abraham “went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land” (Hebrews 11:9), and believers are “sojourners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11). The Septuagint used *paroikos* and *prosēlytos* for the Hebrew *ger*. Finally, *monē* (μονή), from *menō*, means **a place to stay**: “In my Father's house are many **rooms**” (John 14:2), and “we will come to him and make our **home** with him” (John 14:23).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: **Abide or remain?** The KJV and ESV say “**Abide** in me” (John 15:4); the NIV and NLT say “**Remain** in me”. *Menō* means both. “Abide” keeps the familiar church word and its sense of living somewhere; “remain” is clearer modern English but can sound like simply not leaving. Neither fully brings out the picture of staying with a friend or host.

**Mansions or rooms?** The KJV has “In my Father's house are many **mansions**” (John 14:2). This comes from the Latin Bible's *mansiones*, which meant **stopping places, lodgings** (from *manere*, “to remain”), just like the Greek *monē*. Over time English “mansion” came to mean a grand house, so modern versions say “rooms”. The same Greek word returns in John 14:23 (“make our **abode** with him”, KJV; “make our **home** with him”, ESV): the Father and the Son come to live with the believer now.

**Dwelt or pitched his tent?** In John 1:14 most versions say “**dwelt** among us”, and the NIV says “made his **dwelling** among us”. These are accurate, but the tent picture, and its link to the Tabernacle, is easy to miss.

**Dwell or return?** Psalm 23:6 ends “I will **dwell** in the house of the LORD forever.” The Hebrew vowels read *veshavti*, which normally means “**I shall return**”. The Greek translators and most English versions read it as “dwell”, a word with nearly the same letters, which fits the parallel with Psalm 27:4. Some scholars prefer “I shall return (to the house of the LORD)”; either way the hope is to be at home with God for life.

**Lodging for the night.** In Psalm 30:5 the KJV says “weeping may **endure** for a night”. That is a good English idiom, but the Hebrew *yalin* pictures weeping as a guest who **lodges** for one night and leaves in the morning.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In Israel's world, **hospitality** was a sacred duty. A traveller who entered a tent or house was fed and protected, even at cost, as Abraham did for his three visitors (Genesis 18:1–8). To “sojourn in God's tent” (Psalm 15:1) meant to come under the protection of the greatest Host. Israel also remembered that they themselves had been *gerim*, guests and outsiders in Egypt, so they were to welcome others.

The Tabernacle stood **in the centre of the camp**, with the tribes around it (Numbers 2). God lived among his people as a neighbour. The yearly booths of Sukkot reminded each family of the wilderness journey. At that feast in Jesus' day, water was poured out in the Temple, and it was then that Jesus cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). John calls the feast *skēnopēgia*, “tent-pitching” (John 7:2).

In the Greco-Roman world, travellers stayed in inns or with friends, and staying under someone's roof created **lasting bonds**. A *paroikos* was a resident foreigner with limited rights. Early Christians called their local communities *paroikiai*, “groups of sojourners”, and that word, through Latin, gave English the word **parish**. The church was a community of guests on the way to God's city, living by his hospitality.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: staying with Jesus
p: In John's Gospel, abiding is **friendship that lasts**. The Spirit descended on Jesus and “**remained** on him” (John 1:32). Jesus says, “If you **abide** in my word, you are truly my disciples” (John 8:31), and “As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. **Abide** in my love” (John 15:9). Like a branch staying in the vine, the disciple draws life from Jesus and bears fruit (John 15:5).

John's first letter makes it practical: “whoever says he **abides** in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked” (1 John 2:6), and “God is love, and whoever **abides** in love abides in God, and God **abides** in him” (1 John 4:16). Paul speaks of God's Spirit who “**dwells** in you” (Romans 8:9, 11), and of the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). The God who once pitched his tent in the camp now makes his home in his people.

sections.h: Living it out
p: **Stay with Jesus.** Abiding is not a rare feeling but a daily habit of staying near him: listening to his words, talking with him in prayer, obeying his commands and remaining in his love, like friends who keep visiting each other's homes.

**Live as a guest and a host.** You are God's guest, living under his protection, and you are also called to be a host. Open your home and your table to strangers, newcomers and lonely people, as God opened his tent to you.
**Make room for God's presence together.** The Shekhinah rests where people gather around God's word. Find two or three others to read Scripture and pray with regularly.

rows.original: μείνατε ἐν ἐμοί, κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν
rows.literal: stay in me, and I in you
rows.common: Remain in me, as I also remain in you (NIV)
rows.why: “Remain” is clearer than the older “abide”, but both lose the everyday sense of staying with a friend or host.

rows.common: In my Father's house are many mansions (KJV)
rows.why: The KJV followed the Latin mansiones, “lodgings”; later “mansion” came to mean a grand house, so modern versions say “rooms”.
“Dwelt” is accurate and simple, but it hides the Tabernacle picture behind John's verb.

rows.literal: and I shall return to (or dwell in) the house of the LORD
rows.common: I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever (KJV)
rows.why: The Hebrew vowels say “return”; the Greek and most English versions read “dwell”, which fits Psalm 27:4.

rows.literal: in the evening weeping comes to lodge (for the night)
rows.common: weeping may endure for a night (KJV)
rows.why: “Endure” is good English, but the picture of weeping as a guest who leaves at dawn is lost.

diagrams.title: God's dwelling with people across the Bible

steps.d: God walks with the first humans (Genesis 3:8).
God dwells (shakhan) in the mishkan in the centre of the camp (Exodus 25:8).
God's glory fills the house in Jerusalem (1 Kings 8:10–11).
The Word pitches his tent among us (John 1:14).
The Father and Son make their home with believers; the Spirit dwells in them (John 14:23; Romans 8:9).
The dwelling place of God is with man for ever (Revelation 21:3).

verses.text: And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst.
He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty.
O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill?
And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.
Abide in me, and I in you.
If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.
Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people.

keyPoints: Yashav means to sit and so to live somewhere; God himself is his people's dwelling place (Psalm 90:1).
Shakhan gives mishkan (Tabernacle) and shakhen (neighbour): God came to live in the middle of the camp.
Gur and lin picture staying as a protected guest and lodging for the night.
Sukkot reminds Israel every year that God sheltered them in booths.
Menō is the everyday word for staying with someone; “Abide in me” is the language of friendship.
John 1:14 says the Word “pitched his tent” among us, echoing the Tabernacle.
KJV “mansions” (John 14:2) comes from Latin mansiones, “lodgings”, the same word as “home” in John 14:23.
reflect: What would “staying with Jesus” look like in the ordinary hours of your day?
When have you experienced weeping as a guest that left in the morning?
Who could you welcome into your home or table as God has welcomed you?

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word mishkan, Tabernacle, literally mean?
quiz.why: Mishkan comes from shakhan, to dwell; it was the tent where God dwelt among Israel.

quiz.q: Which word from the root of shakhan also means “neighbour”?
quiz.why: Shakhen is the one who dwells next to you (Proverbs 27:10).

quiz.q: What does the Greek verb in John 1:14, eskēnōsen, picture?
quiz.why: Skēnoō comes from skēnē, tent, and recalls the Tabernacle.

quiz.q: Why does the KJV say “many mansions” in John 14:2?
options: It follows the Latin mansiones, meaning lodgings
quiz.why: Latin mansio meant a staying place; the Greek monē means the same, and “rooms” is a closer modern rendering.

quiz.q: In John 1:38–39, what were the first disciples asking when they said “Where are you staying (menō)?”
options: Where Jesus lodged, so they could be with him
Which Temple court he taught in
Which city he was born in
quiz.why: Menō is the ordinary word for staying as a guest; they stayed with him that day.

terms.def: To sit, stay or dwell; to settle and live somewhere.
To settle or dwell; the root of mishkan (Tabernacle) and Shekhinah.
The Tabernacle, literally God's “dwelling place”.
Later Jewish word for God's dwelling presence among his people.
A sojourner or resident foreigner, living under another's protection.
A booth or temporary hut used at the Feast of Booths (Sukkot).
Greek for stay, remain, abide; used in “Abide in me”.
Greek for a place to stay or a home (John 14:2, 23).
